To define $ \Delta S_{conf} $ we begin by comparing the adsorption of alkanes in five different zeolite structures: MFI, CHA, TON, FAU, and MOR. Depicted in Figure 2A is the relationship between the entropy of an adsorbed molecule (alkanes and permanent gases) and its gas-phase entropy, where the molecular entropy on the surface never exceeds that in the gas phase. While a significant loss in entropy occurs in all five zeolites, the absolute loss in entropy is distinct for each framework. Adsorbates in TON exhibit the largest loss in entropy upon adsorption, while FAU results in the smallest entropic losses. If the molecules were to behave as immobile adsorbates on the surface, the entropy lost upon adsorption ( $ \Delta S_{ads} $) can be approximated to be equal to three degrees of translational freedom, $ ^{3,35,36} $ which can be calculated from statistical mechanics using the Sackur–Tetrode equation $ ^{37} $

ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

The turnover rates of olefin formation during cyclohexanol (CyOH) dehydration within the autoclave reactor initially increase with the local ionic strength within a micropore, and further decrease along ionic strength promotion, shown as a volcano-shaped dependence of TOFs on the ionic strength of zeolites. The local ionic environments with moderate-to-high ionic strength alter the adsorption of uncharged reactants, and stabilize surface intermediates and positively charge the transition states, which eventually increase the reaction rates. But the formation and size of the H₃O⁺(H₂O)ₙ₋₁ in the zeolite pores limit the adsorption of CyOH, e.g., size exclusion effects, and decrease reaction rates. On the other hand, the higher ionic strength results in increased excess chemical potentials of the charged transition states, which in turn raises the activation Gibbs free energies²¹⁻²⁵. In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: occ_vol_confinement_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The ratio of occupiable pore volume per mass (AV) to the guest's specific molecular volume (Vol/MW) is the dominant determinant of adsorption entropy loss: decreasing this ratio (tighter confinement) monotonically increases s_ads loss per R, and a model using the full 14 inputs with this descriptor re-expressed as a log confinement ratio will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the raw-input baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01/E02: entropy loss upon adsorption scales with the loss of accessible translational configurational volume. Framework confinement is captured by occupiable volume (AV) and the guest size by molecular volume (Vol) and mass (MW); their log ratio is a dimensionless confinement measure (Sackur–Tetrode-type translational entropy loss). Source evidence: occupiable volume alone predicts confined entropy (E02); mechanism extension to a size-matched ratio is inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If replacing the raw 14-input feature set's nonlinear mapping with the log(AV·MW/Vol) re-expression raises (or does not lower) the MAE of entropy loss/R versus the published full-input baseline, or if residuals show systematic structure-specific bias (e.g., FAU vs TON) not captured by the ratio, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_anisotropy_pore_match
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss depends not only on confinement volume but on the match between molecular shape anisotropy (SPAN/GeDi) and the pore aperture-to-length ratio (lsd_f/lsd_p): adsorbates with high elongation in tubular pores (large descriptor value) lose more rotational entropy than predicted by volume-only confinement, improving MAE of entropy loss/R when this term is included.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E04 (shape selectivity in tubular pore systems, branched vs linear alkanes), E07 (molecular symmetry affects mobility under confinement), and E01 (rotational entropy fractions differ among frameworks). Elongated molecules in one-dimensional channels have restricted rotational degrees of freedom beyond what volumetric confinement captures; SPAN/GeDi encodes molecular elongation and lsd_f/lsd_p encodes pore channel character. This coupling term is our inference, not established in the sources.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this term does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R, or if the improvement is not concentrated in tubular-pore frameworks (TON, MOR, MFI-type systems) as the mechanism predicts, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_area_density_penalty
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss is governed by a balance between guest–wall contact intensity and pore rigidity: strong contact per pore volume (LabuteASA/(AV·density), framework surface density at native scale) increases entropy loss, while framework flexibility (larger PBF relative to pore diameter lsd_f) mitigates it, so this product term improves MAE of entropy loss/R beyond volume-only descriptors.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference combining E02 (contact/accessible surface determines translational restriction) with E06 and E10 (framework flexibility allows guest-induced deformation, partially restoring configurational freedom and reducing entropy loss). The ratio LabuteASA/(AV·density) is a re-expression of existing numerical scales describing wall proximity; PBF/lsd_f acts as a flexibility-to-constraint counter-term. No source states this combined relation; it is our proposed mechanism.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the coefficient structure implied by the mechanism (positive weight on the contact term, negative on the flexibility ratio, tested via ablation of the product structure within the network) does not hold, or if MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve over both the raw baseline and the volume-only descriptor of Proposal 1, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: aniso_confinement_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R scales with the confinement volume ratio (AV relative to guest specific volume, the retained round-1 signal) multiplied by a compactness factor Vol/(LabuteASA+1): molecules with large internal volume relative to their external surface area (low surface-to-volume, i.e., near-spherical, compact guests) lose more configurational entropy under a given volumetric confinement than elongated guests, because compact shapes retain fewer reorientation microstates when wall contact becomes unavoidable. Including this compactness-weighted confinement term with the full 14 inputs will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below the retained baseline value of 0.5472.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference: E01/E02 establish (known) that confinement volume governs entropy loss; E04 and E07 indicate shape and symmetry modulate mobility under confinement (source evidence for shape dependence of confined motion). The surface-to-volume ratio is our proposed compactness measure distinguishing which guests, at equal confinement ratio, are most entropically penalized. This is a new combination, not established in the sources.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve below 0.5472, or if the improvement is not concentrated on compact (low SPAN/GeDi or low surface-to-volume) adsorbates as the mechanism predicts, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: aperture_gating_severity
descriptor_candidates.formula: exp(-lsd_f / lsd_p) * log(1 + AV * density / MW)
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The residual entropy loss unexplained by occupiable volume is controlled by aperture gating severity: the exponential sensitivity exp(-lsd_f/lsd_p) encodes how severely the pore aperture (lsd_f) blocks passage relative to the pore path length/persistence (lsd_p), and multiplying by the logarithmic pore loading-capacity proxy log(1+AV*density/MW) predicts that small-aperture, long-channel frameworks (small lsd_f/lsd_p) impose disproportionally larger translational entropy loss than cavity-type frameworks at equal occupiable volume. Adding this gating-severity term with the full 14 inputs will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5472, with gains concentrated in small-pore tubular frameworks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 shows TON (tubular, small-aperture) has the largest and FAU (large cavities) the smallest entropy loss, beyond what V_occ alone explains; E07 describes aperture-controlled ('trapdoor') transport, indicating windows are the kinetic bottleneck restricting configurational access. The exponential aperture-to-path form is our inference of how window restriction, not total volume, controls the residual translational entropy loss.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R does not drop below 0.5472, or if residual improvement is not framework-type dependent (i.e., it improves uniformly across cavity and channel frameworks without correlation with lsd_f/lsd_p), the gating-severity mechanism is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: inertia_accessibility_decoupling
descriptor_candidates.formula: log(1 + PMI2 / PMI1) + log(1 + sqrt(PMI3 / PMI2) * (PBF / (Vol / MW)))
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Rotational entropy loss upon confinement is governed by the decoupling between a guest's principal-moment asymmetry and the pore's steric hindrance: the logarithmic moment anisotropy log(1+PMI2/PMI1) captures how many distinct rotational orientations a molecule effectively possesses, and the term log(1+sqrt(PMI3/PMI2)*(PBF/(Vol/MW))) captures how strongly the pore breadth parameter (PBF) restricts reorientation of an asymmetric rotor relative to the guest's specific volume. Frameworks/molecule pairs with high combined value will show rotational entropy loss exceeding the volume-based prediction; including both terms with the full 14 inputs will reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5472.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E01 reports rotational entropy fractions differ across frameworks and that the shape–confinement relation within ΔS_conf 'remains to be determined'; E07 shows molecular symmetry affects confined mobility; E05 notes rotational degrees of freedom are reduced under confinement by a fixed correction. The use of principal moments of inertia as the shape/symmetry variable and the coupling to PBF and specific volume is our inference, proposing a mechanism for the unresolved rotational part of ΔS_conf.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve below 0.5472, or if ablation shows the PMI terms contribute nothing once the round-1 volume ratio is present (i.e., the anisotropy terms are collinear with volumetric confinement), the rotational-decoupling hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The rotational fraction of entropy loss is governed by a rotor-quenching index: the product PBF * sqrt(PMI3/(Vol*MW)) measures how strongly the pore breadth parameter (PBF) suppresses reorientation of a guest whose largest principal moment of inertia (PMI3) is large relative to its mass-normalized volume (Vol*MW). Inference: expressing the unresolved rotational part via PMI3 normalized by molecular mass and volume, gated by pore breadth PBF through a saturating exponential (analogous to free-rotor-to-hindered-rotor crossover), is our proposed mechanism and is not established in the sources.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve below 0.5472, or if ablation shows the exponential term is redundant with the retained volume-confinement ratio (no distinct residual structure along the PBF*sqrt(PMI3/(Vol*MW)) axis), the rotor-quenching hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.formula: minimum((lsd_f / lsd_p) ** 2, 1) * log(1 + (Vol / MW) / AV) / (1 + PBF / lsd_p)
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss is the product of a channel-character gate and a flexibility-relieved confinement penalty: (lsd_f/lsd_p)^2 capped at 1 distinguishes one-dimensional tubular pores (small aperture-to-persistence ratio, entropy loss concentrated at windows) from cavity frameworks (ratio saturates at 1); log(1+(Vol/MW)/AV) is the inverted confinement ratio (penalty grows as guest specific volume approaches occupiable volume); and division by (1+PBF/lsd_p) encodes that frameworks whose pore breadth is large relative to the pore persistence allow partial configurational recovery, reducing the penalty. descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve below 0.5472, or if improvement is uniform across cavity and channel frameworks rather than correlated with the capped (lsd_f/lsd_p)^2 gate (or if the PBF/lsd_p relief denominator shows the wrong-signed residual trend, i.e., more flexible frameworks suffer larger entropy loss), the gate-penalty-relief mechanism is falsified.
